assertions.text: Discount ladder, and traveller eligibility are in separate tables. Rolling window counting as a third table is desirable.
assertions.evidence: Response provides only 2 @TableTest methods: childAlwaysReceivesFlatTwentyPercentDiscount and adultAndSeniorAccumulateDiscountByRecentTicketCount. The expected output specifies 3 separate tables for discount ladder, traveller eligibility, and 30-day rolling window counting; the response combines discount ladder with traveller eligibility in the adult/senior table and omits a dedicated rolling window counting table.

assertions.text: Children's flat 20% discount is represented — either as a row in the eligibility table or a separate note. It does not follow the ladder.
assertions.evidence: First table shows multiple rows all with 20% discount for CHILD type: 'Child, no prior trips | CHILD | 0 | 20' through 'Child, above adult max | CHILD | 45 | 20', demonstrating the flat 20% is independent of trip count.

assertions.text: The discount ladder has multiple tiers derived from the 'every fifth trip' rule, with boundary values or value sets showing which ticket counts produce which discount. The maximum 40% discount is represented.
assertions.evidence: Adult/senior table shows 8 tiers: 0% (0-4 tickets), 5% (5-9), 10% (10-14), 15% (15-19), 20% (20-24), 25% (25-29), 30% (30-34), 35% (35-39), and 40% maximum shown at 'Maximum reached — ticket 40 | {ADULT, SENIOR} | 40 | 40' and 'Above maximum, capped at 40% | {ADULT, SENIOR} | 50 | 40'.

assertions.text: The 30-day rolling window boundary is tested: a ticket at exactly 30 days is included, at 31 days is excluded.
assertions.evidence: The adult/senior table tests different recentTickets counts (0, 4, 5, 10, ..., 50) but contains no test cases explicitly checking the 30-day time boundary (e.g., a ticket at exactly 30 days old vs. 31 days old). The description mentions '30 days' but no test row isolates this boundary.

assertions.text: Eligibility uses human-readable values (yes/no or equivalent) rather than raw true/false. TypeConverter or similar mechanism mentioned.
assertions.evidence: While tables use human-readable values (CHILD, ADULT, SENIOR, and discount percentages), TypeConverter is not mentioned anywhere in the code, annotations, design decisions, or dependencies section.

assertions.text: Value sets in the tier table contain exactly the values that produce the same discount. No cross-tier contamination.
assertions.evidence: The adult/senior table uses individual boundary rows (4→0%, 5→5%, 9→5%, 10→10%, etc.) rather than value sets grouping counts per tier. The design decisions explicitly state: 'Adult/Senior table pins every boundary pair.'

assertions.text: @DisplayName is present on test methods, OR method names read as clear descriptive titles when converted from camelCase/snake_case.
assertions.evidence: Method names read as clear descriptive titles: 'childAlwaysReceivesFlatTwentyPercentDiscount' and 'adultAndSeniorAccumulateDiscountByRecentTicketCount'. No @DisplayName annotation is present, but the camelCase names are self-explanatory.

assertions.text: @Description is present on at least the class or the tier method and provides context beyond what the table rows already express — such as the discount ladder structure, eligibility rules, or application context.
assertions.evidence: Both methods have @Description: Children's states 'Children receive a flat 20% discount... The recentTickets count has no effect', and adult/senior's explains 'Every 5 tickets moves one step up the discount ladder (+5%)... measured at the time of purchase' plus notes ambiguity about current-ticket inclusion—all context beyond the table rows themselves.

assertions.text: TypeConverterSources is used for at least one human-readable conversion (yes/no, or rolling window notation).
assertions.evidence: No TypeConverterSources annotation or TypeConverter import appears in the code. Tables display raw enum values (CHILD, ADULT, SENIOR) and plain integer percentages without converter mechanism.

assertions.text: Annotations appear in order: @DisplayName (if present), @Description (if present), @TableTest — not any other order.
assertions.evidence: Both test methods follow the correct order: @Description appears first, then @TableTest. @DisplayName is absent, so the order is @Description, @TableTest—correct per the rule.

assertions.text: If @Description is present and the text is longer than a single short line, it uses a text block (triple-quoted string """), not string concatenation with +. Passes if @Description is absent.
assertions.evidence: Both @Description annotations use triple-quoted strings: @Description("""...Children receive a flat 20%....""") and @Description("""...Every 5 tickets moves...."""), not string concatenation.

assertions.text: The discount ladder table uses value sets for the ticket count column to group counts within the same tier (e.g. {5, 6, 7, 8, 9} or {5, 9} for min/max → 5%) — not one row per boundary value.
assertions.evidence: The adult/senior discount ladder table uses individual rows for each boundary: 'Just below first threshold | {ADULT, SENIOR} | 4 | 0', 'First tier — ticket 5 | {ADULT, SENIOR} | 5 | 5', 'Just below second threshold | {ADULT, SENIOR} | 9 | 5', etc. Design decisions state: 'Adult/Senior table pins every boundary pair.'

assertions.text: The tier-to-discount mapping is expressed once — not repeated across multiple tables. A price application table (if present) should test the arithmetic (base price × discount → final price) without re-enumerating which ticket counts map to which tier.
assertions.evidence: The tier-to-discount mapping (0% for 0–4 tickets, 5% for 5–9 tickets, ..., 40% for ≥40 tickets) is expressed once in the adult/senior table. No separate price application or tier re-enumeration table is present.
